country.name: United States
country.kicker: A continental country with worldwide reach.

overview.summary: A federal republic whose huge internal market, immigration, and global connections helped build exceptional economic influence. Its fifty states contain sharply different landscapes, histories, and ways of life.
overview.geography: The contiguous states stretch between the Atlantic and Pacific, with Canada to the north and Mexico to the south. Alaska and Hawaii extend the country into the Arctic and central Pacific.

whyItMatters.title: The world’s financial reference point
whyItMatters.text: The dollar and US financial markets link American economic decisions to borrowing, trade, and savings around the world.

whyItMatters.title: Ideas that travel
whyItMatters.text: Universities, technology companies, media, and scientific institutions give the country influence well beyond its physical borders.

stories.summary: A currency becomes international when many people find it useful at the same time.

sections.title: Deep markets, useful assets
sections.text: Large, liquid financial markets offer places to borrow, invest, and hold reserves. US Treasury securities are important in that system.

sections.title: A network that reinforces itself
sections.text: If trading partners invoice and borrow in dollars, others have a reason to do the same. That network gives US monetary policy effects far beyond the country.

stories.takeaway: The dollar’s role is supported by institutions, markets, and network effects, not simply by America’s size.

stories.question: How much did geography help?

phrasings: Did geography make the United States powerful?

was the US just lucky with its map?
What role did geography play in the rise of the United States?

stories.summary: The map created opportunities. People and institutions determined how they were used.

sections.title: A large connected interior
sections.text: Productive farmland, major rivers, and access to two oceans helped support trade and a large internal market. Roads and railways later extended those connections.

sections.title: Expansion was not empty space
sections.text: The territorial growth of the United States involved Indigenous dispossession, slavery, war, and settlement. Geographic advantages cannot be separated from that history.

stories.takeaway: A favorable map helps explain capacity. It does not explain away the costs of building a nation.

stories.summary: Migration is central to the country, but it is not everyone’s origin story.

sections.title: Many routes into American life
sections.text: Successive waves of immigration brought skills, languages, and communities. Foreign-born residents include both naturalized citizens and noncitizens.

sections.title: Different histories of belonging
sections.text: Indigenous peoples preceded the state. Enslaved Africans were brought by force. Immigration rules and citizenship rights have also changed through political conflict.

stories.takeaway: The useful story is about different paths to belonging, not one shared path of arrival.
